query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A minor boron addition (1–2 at%) to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing the alloy’s high strength or its impact-induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline refractory high-entropy alloy produced by arc/vacuum induction melting and homogenization, exhibiting high strength and significant energy release under impact but limited ductility.
generation.intervention: Incorporate 1–2 at% boron into the baseline alloy composition during the same melting and homogenization process used for the control alloy.
generation.conditions: Assess mechanical behavior in quasi-static tensile tests and high-strain-rate impact tests at ambient to elevated temperatures, comparing boron-modified samples to the baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at grain boundaries, enhancing boundary cohesion and reducing grain boundary cracking susceptibility.
generation.mechanism: Boron increases grain boundary cohesion through segregation, lowering boundary energy and suppressing intergranular cracking, thereby improving ductility and uniform deformation while preserving matrix properties that confer high strength and energetic performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced tensile ductility and uniform elongation of the boron-doped alloy relative to the baseline, with comparable high strength and no reduction in energetic release under dynamic loading.
generation.baseline: Undoped refractory high-entropy alloy of similar composition and processing history, with known high strength and energy release but lower ductility.
generation.boundary: Effects may diminish if boron content deviates significantly from 1–2 at%, or under extreme testing conditions (e.g., ultra-high or subambient temperatures).
generation.uncertainty: Direct data on boron doping within the supplied references are lacking, although beneficial effects of boron are suggested by prior research in steels and Ni-based superalloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare baseline and boron-doped test samples under identical melting and homogenization conditions, then perform tensile tests and high-velocity impact tests to compare mechanical properties and energy release.
measurements: Yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation at various temperatures

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If boron addition does not increase ductility or if it significantly reduces either the high strength or impact-induced energy release compared with the baseline alloy, the hypothesis is invalidated.

chosen.conditions: Tensile and high-strain-rate impact testing from ambient to elevated temperatures
chosen.why: Proposed intervention: A minor boron addition (1–2 at%) to the refractory high-entropy alloy to enhance grain-boundary cohesion. Hypothesized mechanism: Boron segregates to grain boundaries, reducing their propensity to crack and increasing overall ductility and uniform plastic deformation. Expected improvement: Enhanced ductility without compromising the base alloy’s high strength or its capacity for impact-induced energy release, as the multi-principal element matrix and its energetic behavior remain intact. Supporting evidence: Previous studies on boron-doped steels and Ni-based superalloys show improved grain boundary strength and ductility from small B additions. Decisive experiment to falsify: Compare mechanical behavior and energy-release characteristics under tension and high-strain-rate impact in both untreated and boron-doped samples; if no improvement in ductility or if energy release is degraded, the hypothesis is invalidated.
